analysis.one_liner: Writes police qualified immunity into federal law, shielding officers and their agencies from civil damages lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in August 2020 with 2 Republican cosponsors, the bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee and expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write the Supreme Court's qualified immunity doctrine into federal statute for police officers sued for violating someone's constitutional rights. A victim could not win money damages unless the law was already so clear that 'every reasonable officer' would have known the conduct was illegal, or a court had already upheld a decision on that exact conduct. It would go beyond current court doctrine by also shielding the officer's agency and local government from liability whenever the officer is immune.
analysis.who_benefits: Law enforcement officers at the federal, state, tribal, and local level, plus the agencies and local governments that employ them. Officers would be personally shielded from damages lawsuits except in the narrowest cases, and their employers would for the first time be shielded whenever the officer is immune — protecting them from jury verdicts and settlement costs in cases of constitutional misconduct.

how_it_helps.text: The bill writes qualified immunity into statute: an officer cannot be found liable if the constitutional right was not 'clearly established' at the time, or if no court had already ruled that the specific conduct was lawful under the Constitution [S2, S3].

It adds a shield that current law does not provide: the law enforcement agency or unit of local government that employed the officer would not be liable if the officer is immune and was acting within the scope of employment [S2, S3].

The bill's own findings state the purpose: protecting officers from 'harassment, distraction, and liability' when they make reasonable mistakes, while retaining accountability for those who are 'plainly incompetent or knowingly violate the law' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Victims of police misconduct. A person whose constitutional rights were violated could recover damages only where the law was already unmistakably clear on that exact conduct — which in practice means victims of novel or first-of-its-kind misconduct would have no remedy against the officer, and now not against the department either.

drawbacks.text: Codifying qualified immunity in statute would lock it in by law, preventing courts from later narrowing or abolishing the doctrine as they can when it is judge-made [S2, S3].

By requiring that 'every reasonable law enforcement officer' would have understood the conduct was illegal, the bill sets a stricter standard than the existing doctrine, making recovery harder for plaintiffs [S3].

Extending immunity to agencies and local governments is a genuine expansion: under current doctrine, municipalities can be held liable for unconstitutional policies even when the individual officer is immune, so victims would lose an entire avenue of recovery [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's defenders argue officers making honest mistakes should not face personal financial ruin, and that shielding governments saves taxpayers settlement costs. Those are real considerations. But the cost side is heavier: the bill does not merely preserve the existing balance — it hardens it in statute, sets a stricter bar for victims, and newly insulates the departments that set the policies. Because courts could no longer recalibrate the doctrine, an egregious violation with no clear precedent would leave the victim with no remedy at all.

outcome.mechanism: Rep. Banks introduced it in August 2020 and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled a hearing or vote; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Banks (R-IN) introduced the Qualified Immunity Act of 2020 on August 7, 2020, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1, S5].
Two Republican House members cosponsored the bill [S4].

The bill would amend the civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to codify qualified immunity for law enforcement officers sued in their individual capacity, and would also exempt their agencies and local governments from liability when the officer is immune and acting within the scope of employment [S2, S3].
The House Judiciary Committee took no further action after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill expired with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement officers and agencies gained nothing, but nothing changed either. Because the bill died, victims of police misconduct kept the existing court system — including the possibility that courts could narrow qualified immunity over time — and departments were not newly shielded from liability. Police unions and their allies lost a chance to lock the doctrine into statute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Victims of police misconduct kept their remedies

for.name: Jim Banks
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 7, 2020 to codify qualified immunity for law enforcement officers and shield their agencies from liability [S1, S3].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after the August 2020 referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — letting the bill die at the end of the Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on. This came in a Congress where the Democratic-led House had just passed the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act, which moved the opposite way by eliminating qualified immunity.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill would turn judicial qualified immunity into federal statute, locking in officers' personal protection from damages lawsuits in a way courts could no longer adjust. Officers' interest in avoiding personal liability runs directly against victims' ability to be compensated for constitutional violations.

industries.industry: Local governments and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill would newly shield departments and local governments from liability whenever an officer is immune, saving them settlement and verdict costs. But that savings comes from removing a deterrent that constrains police practices, and payouts already come largely from taxpayers either way.

Plaintiffs' civil rights attorneys would see most §1983 cases against officers become unwinnable, shrinking their practice. Their interest in bringing these suits runs alongside victims' access to remedies.
